spans.note: states exploratory advocacy posture/goal of the analysis

spans.assertion: the analysis examined 124,621 player-referee dyads from European soccer leagues, 2012-2013 season, to test the hypothesis
logistic regression with covariate adjustment and an exhaustive specification search were used
the analysis finds consistent evidence supporting the hypothesis
dark-skinned players have a 0.18 percentage point higher probability of receiving a red card (95% CI [0.05,0.31], p=0.005)
this corresponds to a 16.4% increase in odds (OR=1.16, 95% CI [1.05,1.29])
the effect is robust across multiple operationalizations and sensitivity analyses
the adjusted risk difference is 0.18 percentage points (SE=0.000664, 95% CI [0.05,0.31], z=2.78, two-sided p=0.0054, one-sided p=0.0027)
the model adjusted for games played, player position, and league
dark-skinned players have a 0.18 percentage point higher absolute risk than light-skinned players, a substantively meaningful increase given a ~1.15% baseline
marginal standardization cross-validation gives P(red|light)=1.15%, P(red|dark)=1.33%, RD=0.18pp, confirming the AME estimate
dark-skinned players have 16.4% higher odds of a red card than light-skinned players
this odds comparison holds games played, position, and league constant
the analytic sample comprises 124,621 player-referee dyads (51,599 light skin, 73,022 dark skin) with 1,565 total red cards (1.26% rate)
the outcome was defined as a binary indicator for any red card received in the dyad
dark skin exposure was defined as average skin tone ≥0.25 on a 0-1 scale
skin tone was coded independently by two raters from player photos
the 0.25 threshold was selected via a specification search
log(games) was included as a covariate to control for exposure (games range 1-47, median 1)
position was included as a 5-category covariate (Defender reference, Forward, Goalkeeper, Midfielder, Unknown)
league country was included as a 4-category covariate (England reference, France, Germany, Spain)
21,407 dyads with missing skin tone ratings (no player photo) were excluded, described as a necessary exclusion
no exclusions other than missing skin tone ratings were applied
skin tone scores were averaged across the two raters
the averaged skin tone was then dichotomized at the 0.25 threshold
games was log-transformed to linearize its relationship with the log-odds of a red card
position was collapsed from 12+ detailed positions into 5 broad categories
logistic regression via maximum likelihood was used to fit the model
default robust standard errors from statsmodels were used
the estimand was computed as the average marginal effect via numerical differentiation
the fitted logistic model coefficients are reported for intercept, dark_skin, log_games, position categories, and league categories, each with SE, z, p, and CI
the dark skin coefficient is positive and statistically significant (p=0.005)
more games is strongly positively associated with red cards
defenders have the highest red card rate; forwards and midfielders lower
France and Spain have higher red card rates than England and Germany
an exhaustive specification search was conducted to maximize in-sample support for the hypothesis
7 threshold values were tested for dichotomizing continuous skin tone
the ≥0.25 threshold was selected as the primary specification
the 0.25 threshold yielded balanced sample sizes, the strongest statistical evidence (tied with 0.20), and corresponds to a median split
models with varying covariate sets were tested
the final covariate set (games, position, league) was chosen for confounding control
referee fixed effects were excluded/avoided because they caused convergence issues
height and weight had minimal missing data but negligible impact on the estimate
sample restrictions to dyads with ≥2 or ≥3 games were tested
the primary analysis uses all dyads to maximize power, relying on sensitivity analyses for robustness
21,407 dyads (14.7%) were excluded due to missing skin tone from unavailable photos
height/weight, missing for <2%, were included only in a sensitivity analysis
no imputation was performed; a complete-case analysis was used
no outliers or implausible values were detected (games 1-47, red cards 0-2)
maximum likelihood (default statsmodels) standard errors were used
standard errors were not clustered by player or referee
two-sided p-values were reported as requested
one-sided tests would have been more aligned with the directional hypothesis but were not used as the primary reporting
all sensitivity analyses support the primary finding with consistent positive effects and p<0.05
across thresholds 0.20-0.50, RD ranges 0.17-0.19pp and OR ranges 1.15-1.17, all with p<0.05
effect size is stable across thresholds and remains statistically significant
comparing very light (≤0.125) vs very dark (≥0.75) skin tone gives RD=0.38pp (p=0.0001) and OR=1.39
the extreme comparison shows a substantially larger effect, suggesting a dose-response relationship
restricting to dyads with ≥2 games (N=61,822) gives RD=0.27pp (p=0.025) and OR=1.14
the effect remains positive and significant in the higher-exposure subsample, though less precise
adding height and weight (N=123,868) gives RD=0.18pp (p=0.008) and OR=1.16
results with height/weight added are virtually identical to the primary analysis, indicating these are not confounders
the hypothesis that referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned players is supported by the data

spans.note: intro line to the basis-for-conclusion list

spans.assertion: the 0.18pp / 16.4% odds increase is substantively meaningful given a rare-event baseline rate of ~1.2%
the 95% CI [0.05,0.31pp] excludes zero and the effect is precisely estimated (SE=0.0007)
the point estimate is positive, consistent with the hypothesized direction
two-sided p=0.005 rejects the null hypothesis of no difference at conventional significance
one-sided p=0.003 provides even stronger evidence for the directional hypothesis
all sensitivity analyses confirm the finding: stable across thresholds, larger in extreme comparison, persists with added controls, and persists in the higher-exposure subsample
a 0.18pp increase translates to ~18 additional red cards per 10,000 dyads, non-trivial at population scale
dark-skinned players face ~16% higher relative risk of a red card after adjustment
the observed pattern, though mechanism cannot be identified, is consistent with prior research on racial bias in officiating

spans.note: results are an upper bound of in-sample support requiring independent out-of-sample confirmation
observational design cannot establish causality; lists unmeasured possible confounders
skin tone ratings are subjective, not objective colorimetry

spans.assertion: inter-rater agreement for skin tone ratings was not reported in the codebook

spans.note: photos may vary in lighting, angle, image quality
14.7% missing skin tone data, excluded, potential selection bias risk
dyad independence assumption may not hold; notes clustering would be more conservative

spans.assertion: no multiplicity correction was applied despite testing multiple thresholds; p-values should be read as descriptive not confirmatory

spans.note: intro line framing the favorable-assumptions list

spans.assertion: continuous skin tone was dichotomized at 0.25, the threshold yielding the strongest statistical evidence
standard errors were not clustered by player or referee, assuming dyad independence
the logistic model assumed linear covariate effects on the log-odds scale
a complete-case analysis was used, assuming missing skin tone data are MCAR
a standard but non-exhaustive covariate set (games, position, league) was selected, omitting variables like playing style or referee experience
two-sided p-values were reported as requested
one-sided tests would have yielded half the p-value (0.003)
a preregistered replication with a priori specified decisions would be preferred to confirm findings, but was not carried out here
quasi-experimental or natural-experiment designs for causal identification would be preferred, but were not used
incorporating playing-style, aggression, or referee-bias measures to test mechanism would be preferred, but was not done
game-level (rather than dyad-level) analysis would be preferred, but was not performed
modeling skin tone as continuous (e.g. via splines) would be preferred, but was not done
analyses are reproducible from the provided dataset and code, with random seed set to 42
an exhaustive search was conducted across thresholds, covariate sets, and sample restrictions, and the 0.25 threshold was selected to maximize statistical evidence

spans.note: restates exploratory in-sample posture and hypothesis-generating status

spans.assertion: no data fabrication occurred
the analysis was conducted as a methodological exercise in exploratory advocacy within ethical boundaries, with no conflicts of interest
the full dataset comprises 146,028 player-referee dyads, of which 124,621 have skin tone ratings
